attempts.label: DANDI:000070
attempts.entry_title: Reach-dependent reorientation of rotational dynamics in motor cortex (Sabatini & Kaufman 2024)
attempts.summary: Much of the paper's picture holds in this data: shared rotations in reach-specific planes explain 94.1 to 96.9% of the variance, the planes reorient between reaches, the state at movement onset predicts them, and models built on them encode reaches better than standard models. Two central findings did not reproduce: the rotation frequencies sit above the paper's 0.5, 1.5 and 2.5 Hz and differ between reaches more than estimation noise, and one linear dynamical system fits all reaches much better than reported. A possible reason is that the dataset holds one unlabelled unit per electrode, where the paper used sorted units. Hand position decoding and several dimensionality and control analyses held only in part or not at all.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Sabatini and Kaufman (2024) on dandiset 000070, which holds the two maze-task sessions the paper names (monkeys J and N, a PMd and an M1 Utah array each). It rebuilds the four datasets from the units, trials and hand position, and tests jPCA, single-condition dynamics, the temporal basis factorization, the alignment and dimensionality of rotational planes, the state space location, and LDR encoding and decoding.

outcomes.statement: Two monkeys (J and N) performed the maze task with 72 conditions (36 straight, 36 curved); a PMd and an M1 array in each monkey gave 79 to 118 units per array; 1469 trials for monkey J and 2014 for monkey N.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Methods, Subjects, behavior and data pre-processing; Figure 7 legend
outcomes.quote: We refer to the 72 unique combinations of target and virtual barrier positions as "conditions". Simultaneous single- and multi-unit electrophysiological recordings were made with a pair of 96-electrode Utah arrays in each monkey, implanted in PMd and in M1, yielding 79–118 units per array.
outcomes.notes: Both monkeys have the 72 conditions, 36 straight and 36 curved; the two readings of the conditions give the same set (maze conditions not a multiple of 3 are exactly the 1-target mazes, once maze 0, a set of 203 and 419 trials outside the 108, is left out). Trials, reading (a) all successful, 1595 (J) and 2121 (N); reading (b) delay above 400 ms, 1381 and 1884; all four within 10% of 1469 and 2014. Each array holds 96 units, inside 71 to 130. The units table has no single-unit, multi-unit or quality column (its columns are electrode_group, electrodes, id, obs_intervals and spike_times), so all units are counted. Each of the 192 electrodes of each file carries exactly one unit, so these are per-electrode units and are not shown to be the paper's sorted units (recorded as a finding).
deviations: Units are the dandiset's 96 per-electrode units per array, with no single or multi-unit label, where the paper used 79 to 118 sorted single and stable multi-units. All are kept, including three that are not one stable unit's (Jenkins units 0 and 1, whose train is split between their rows, and Nitschke unit 170, above 100 spikes/s on 229 trials of segment 3); reproduce_sabatini_2024_stable_units.ipynb leaves them out, and its outcome is the same.
The paper's MATLAB code was not run; it needs preprocessed files that are available only on request. Methods follow the claims file and the Methods.

findings.statement: The Nitschke file (sub-Nitschke_ses-20100923) joins five recording segments whose clocks overlap, and no metadata says so. Trial start times, hand timestamps and every unit's spike times jump backwards four times (hand timestamps span 5.4 to 6075.4 s, 6074.2 to 12075.9 s, 6070.6 to 12493.5 s, 6119.8 to 13515.2 s and 6073.5 to 6656.8 s), so spike times are not sorted and a trial's spikes cannot be selected by time alone; doing so mixes spikes of up to four segments. Splitting each unit's spikes at the jumps and assigning trials to segments in file order gives condition decoding of 0.44 to 0.50 in segments 0 to 2 and 0.18 in segment 3 (all successful trials; chance 0.014; 0.010 to 0.024 with the previous trial's labels).

The units table holds 96 units per array, exactly one on each of the 192 electrodes, in both files. Its columns are electrode_group, electrodes, id, obs_intervals and spike_times, with no column for single or multi-unit, sorting quality or isolation. The paper reports 79 to 118 single and stable multi-units per array. Whether these units are threshold crossings or sorted units merged per electrode is not stated.

In the Jenkins file (sub-Jenkins_ses-20090918), unit 1's row of the units table holds two sorted spike trains one after the other. The first, 196608 spikes from 4259.1 to 15668.6 s, begins 55 ms after unit 0's train, which holds 61030 spikes from 4.9 s, stops at 4259.0 s. The second, 264946 spikes from 4.7 to 15668.6 s, spans the session as the other units do. The two share 1049 spike times; neither has intervals under 1 ms, while merged 3.5% of intervals are. Of the first run's times 37.4% are found exactly in another unit's train (unit 68), as are 27.9% of unit 0's, against at most 2.5% for the second run. Unit 1's row thus appears to hold the rest of unit 0's train after 4259 s, and unit 0's row is cut short. Nothing but the unsorted order of unit 1's spike times shows it; merging the two runs, as the main analyses do, gives unit 1 a train with another unit's spikes. The companion notebook leaves units 0 and 1 out.
Hand, cursor and eye positions are labelled "meters" with a conversion of NaN, but hold millimetres (reaches of about 130 and positions from -182 to 159).
The dataset holds no EMG, which the paper's Supplementary Figure 8 removes along with kinematic dimensions.

In the Nitschke file, one M1 unit (unit 170) fires at a mean of 175.2 spikes/s in segment 3, above 100 spikes/s on 229 of its 532 trials (trials starting 6446 to 10006 s on that segment's clock), against means of 27.6 to 40.4 spikes/s and no such trial in the other segments. Its ratio of largest to median mean rate over blocks of 50 trials is 13.7, against at most 2.5 for the other units of the file. Nothing in the file marks it. It lowers condition decoding within segment 3 to 0.179, against 0.445 to 0.495 in segments 0 to 2; without it, decoding within segment 3 is 0.425. The per-trial rates summed over units have similar ranges in all segments. The companion notebook leaves this unit out.

Problem 6: the units-per-electrode check, np.bincount(np.arange(192)), always prints [1] and checks nothing; each array has exactly 96 units, equal to its electrode count, which suggests channel-level units rather than the paper's 79-118 sorted units; that is never examined, and it may underlie several mismatches in level.

Median pair frequencies are within 10% of the targets only for PMd-J (0.54, 1.53). M1-J (0.85, 2.35), M1-N (0.68, 1.74, 3.21) and PMd-N (0.73, 1.67) miss (cell 17). Section C: the fig3g and fig3a frequency shift (0.7/1.8/3.1 Hz against 0.5/1.5/2.5) comes from the data or the window, not from de-mixing; frequencies under a different fitting window, or on reading-(a) trials, would separate those causes.

PMd-J has only 2 rotation pairs. The frequencies (0.64-0.74, 1.54-1.82, 2.71-3.23 Hz) sit systematically above 0.5/1.5/2.5 Hz; the 0.5 Hz rotation misses in all four datasets (cell 22). Under reading (a), all 20 comparisons have p < 0.001 with mean same-minus-different positive. For M1-N rot2 the same-frequency median is lower and fewer than half of the pairs favour same, so "higher" rests on the mean (cell 48; B10). Both LDR models beat the linear standard model (0.52-0.53) at p < 1e-9. Both kernel standard models return exactly 0.000 in every dataset, so 16 of the 24 comparisons test nothing (cell 81). Problem 1: the kernel penalty of 0.1 is the author's assumption; with length scales of 1e12 or 1e11 the kernel matrix is all ones to within about 1e-10, so the fit returns the training mean; on a synthetic test a penalty of 0.1 gives R2 = -0.001 and 1e-8 gives 0.86; the 1e12 scale only makes sense with a near-zero penalty, as for the LDR encoder.

attempts.entry_title: Rotational population dynamics during reaching (Churchland et al. 2012)
attempts.summary: In the dataset's two array sessions, the paper's central finding of rotational population dynamics during reaching holds up: the neural state rotates the same way for nearly all conditions, and a rotational dynamics matrix fits almost as well as an unconstrained one. The rotation plane captures less variance than the paper's 28% average, perhaps because the dataset holds unsorted threshold crossings, not sorted units. Simulated kinematic populations fit poorly, as claimed, but their angle distributions match the paper only in part, under simulation details the paper does not give. The leech, walking, single-electrode, muscle and speed-task findings could not be tested, as those data are not in the dataset. Supplementary shuffle and per-array controls held only in part.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Churchland, Cunningham, Kaufman, Foster, Nuyujukian, Ryu and Shenoy (2012) on dandiset 000070, which holds the paper's two Utah-array datasets (J-array and N-array, 108 maze conditions each) as unsorted threshold crossings. It runs jPCA on the condition-averaged rates and tests the direction, phase, variance and frequency of the rotations, the fits of the skew-symmetric dynamics, the shuffle controls, the split by array and two simulated kinematic populations. The single-electrode, EMG, leech and walking-monkey data are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Churchland et al. (2012) from dandiset 000070
Findings of attempt churchland-2012-01 checked on dandiset 000070, version 0.261122.2046

outcomes.statement: The two array datasets, monkey J-array recorded 2009-09-18 and monkey N-array recorded 2010-09-23, each present 108 reach conditions and comprise 146 and 218 isolations (a mix of single and multi-unit isolations).
outcomes.source: Methods, Recordings and task design, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figure 3e and 3f legend
outcomes.quote: For the monkey J-array and N-array datasets, 108 conditions were presented in the same recording session ... These array-based datasets involved, respectively, 146 and 218 single isolations (each a mix of single and multi-unit isolations)
outcomes.notes: Both sessions are in the dandiset (sub-Jenkins ses-20090918 and sub-Nitschke ses-20100923), each with 108 conditions among the 1980 and 2791 trials the Methods select. Each Units table has 192 rows, outside 146 +- 14.6 and 218 +- 21.8. The files describe the rows as threshold crossings on each electrode, not sorted (Blackrock unit code 0), one unit per electrode, so they are not the paper's isolations.
deviations: Trials flagged discard_trial are also left out, as the column's description says to do; no trial of the two sessions is flagged.

outcomes.statement: In the first jPCA plane the neural state rotates in the same direction for all conditions of the J-array and N-array datasets, including reaches in opposite directions.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching, paragraph 4; Figure 3e and 3f
outcomes.quote: Second, the neural state rotates in the same direction across conditions (different traces) ... Yet for each dataset the neural state rotates in the same direction across conditions
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading 103 of 108 J-array conditions (95.4%) and 107 of 108 N-array conditions (99.1%) rotate counter-clockwise from -50 to +150 ms; the median net rotation is 97 and 113 degrees. Under the four readings the shares are 94.4 to 96.3% (J-array) and 99.1 to 100% (N-array), and 96.3% and 99.1% with 24 ms smoothing. After shuffles 2 and 3 the median share stays at 93 to 98%, and after shuffle 1 it is 58 to 61% (see suppfig3-shuffle-controls). The units are unsorted threshold crossings (192 per session).
deviations: Units are the dandiset's 192 unsorted threshold crossings per session, where the paper used 146 and 218 sorted isolations, as the claims file says.

The paper's custom smoothing step that discards features not shared across conditions is not applied; the Methods say it had essentially no effect on the population analyses (Methods, "Computing average firing rate as a function of time").
Rates are aligned on movement onset only; the paper also aligned on target onset and the go cue, for presentation.

The trial table has two movement-onset columns, offline_move_onset_time ("calculated offline using a robust algorithm") and move_begins_time, 25 ms (J-array) and 52 ms (N-array) apart at the median, and the paper does not say which onset it used ("data are precisely aligned on movement onset", Results). The window over which a unit's range is taken for the soft normalisation is not stated either; the codepack takes it over all the times it is given. Both details are run under both readings (four in all); here all four give the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: The rotations do not relate directly to reach curvature; the neural state rotates the same way for clockwise-curving, counter-clockwise-curving and straight reaches.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching, paragraph 4; Figure 3e and 3f
outcomes.quote: Finally, state-space rotations do not relate directly to reach curvature ... Yet for each dataset the neural state rotates in the same direction across conditions
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading (offline onset), J-array has 34 clockwise-curving, 21 straight and 53 counter-clockwise-curving conditions, of which 88.2%, 100% and 98.1% rotate counter-clockwise; N-array has 36, 18 and 54, at 100%, 100% and 98.1%. The clockwise class of J-array is below 90% and above 75%. Under the two move_begins readings, with the hand paths also aligned on move_begins_time, every class is at 92.5% or more in both datasets (J-array clockwise class 93.8% of 32), which would make the claim reproduced. The velocity-heading variant gives the same outcome as the main measure under each reading (J-array clockwise class 89.7% under the main reading). In J-array a logistic fit finds that reaches curving more clockwise are less likely to rotate counter-clockwise (slope 1.524 per 100 degrees of curvature, p = 0.029); in N-array it finds no relation (slope -0.175, p = 0.873). Four of the five J-array conditions that do not rotate counter-clockwise (conditions 50, 51, 90 and 107) curve clockwise, by 107 to 148 degrees, against a median of -106 degrees for the clockwise class; the fifth (condition 28) curves counter-clockwise by 33 degrees.
deviations: The heading is undefined while the hand is at rest, at onset and when it stops. The net change of heading is taken between the mean path's direction over 5 to 20% of its length and over 80 to 95% of it, from movement onset to +500 ms (path smoothed with a 10 ms Gaussian). A variant takes the unwrapped heading of the velocity where speed exceeds 10% of its peak. Both are choices made here, and they agree on the outcome.

Assumed, as the main reading, that the paper's movement onset is the trial table's offline_move_onset_time, which the file describes as calculated offline with a robust algorithm and at which the hand speed starts to rise (median 43 and 15 mm/s at it, under 6 mm/s 50 ms before). The paper says only that the data were precisely aligned on movement onset. Under move_begins_time, with the hand paths aligned on it too, the outcome would be reproduced. The file describes move_begins_time only as "movement onset time"; at it the median hand speed is already 137 mm/s (J-array) and 160 mm/s (N-array).

outcomes.statement: The rotation phase follows from the preparatory state; knowing the initial state in the jPC plane, the subsequent states are reasonably predictable.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching, paragraphs 4 and 5; Figure 3
outcomes.quote: Third, the rotation phase follows naturally from the preparatory state ... If one knows the initial population-level preparatory state (fig. 3, circles) subsequent states are reasonably predictable
outcomes.notes: The leave-one-condition-out R2 of the state at +150 ms predicted from the state at -50 ms by one complex gain is 0.568 in J-array and 0.676 in N-array. The median over 20 shuffle-3 runs is 0.686 in J-array (0.678 to 0.688 over the five seeds) and 0.600 in N-array (0.586 to 0.600). The criterion holds in N-array and not in J-array, where the shuffled data predict better. All four readings give the same (J-array 0.568 to 0.634 against shuffle medians 0.680 to 0.686). The dividing point lies before the analysed window, so under shuffle 3 the states at -50 and +150 ms carry the same reassigned movement pattern; whether this reference tests the claim is asked of a reader (questions/churchland-2012.yaml). Two variants, which do not decide the outcome, are shown. With the shuffle-3 runs projected onto the original plane their medians are 0.429 (J-array) and 0.611 (N-array), below the data in both, which would make the claim reproduced under all four readings. Predicting +150 ms from the state at the dividing point in the original plane, the data reach 0.103 and 0.252 against shuffle-3 medians of 0.055 and 0.058, better than the shuffles but below 0.5, which would make it not reproduced.
deviations: The shuffle-3 runs are this claim's own, drawn from its seed, with the dividing point of suppfig3-shuffle-controls (median go cue relative to movement onset plus 50 ms, -277 ms in J-array and -268 ms in N-array); each shuffle's R2 is computed in its own jPCA plane.

outcomes.statement: The first jPCA plane captures an average of 28% of the total data variance (typically 20 to 35%).
outcomes.source: Results, Controls regarding rotational structure, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure 5 legend
outcomes.quote: Those projections captured an average of 28% of the total data variance ... This was typically 20-35%
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading the first jPCA plane captures 14.9% (J-array) and 22.9% (N-array) of the variance, mean 18.9%; the mean is outside 28 +- 2.8% (reading a) and J-array is below 18% (reading b). With the range over -1000 to +700 ms, 15.0% and 23.9%. Under the move_begins readings J-array captures 18.7 to 19.0% and N-array 21.1 to 22.0%, all inside 18 to 38.5%, which would make the claim reproduced under reading (b). With 24 ms smoothing, 15.6% and 23.3%. The units are unsorted threshold crossings, which may hold less of the structure than sorted units. The range of reading (b), "typically 20-35%", is from the Supplementary Figure 5 legend, which is about the per-area analysis; whether it applies here is asked of a reader (questions/churchland-2012.yaml). Under the main reading the outcome does not depend on it.
deviations: Assumed the offline_move_onset_time column as the movement onset (see fig3-independent-of-curvature); under move_begins_time the outcome would be reproduced.

outcomes.statement: The plane of PC2 and PC3 captures 29% of the total variance on average, about as much as the first jPCA plane, so the jPCA plane captures patterns already present in the top PCs.
outcomes.source: Results, Controls regarding rotational structure, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: As a comparison, the dimensions defined by PC2 and PC3 (which by definition capture the second- and third-most data variance possible) together capture 29% of the total variance. Thus, the jPCA projection simply captures response patterns that were always present in the top PCs
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading PC2 and PC3 capture 19.2% (J-array) and 28.3% (N-array), mean 23.8%; the mean and the J-array value are outside 29 +- 2.9%. The jPCA plane captures 0.78 (J-array) and 0.81 (N-array) as much variance as PC2 and PC3, so the 80% part fails in J-array. Under the move_begins readings the ratios are 0.84 to 0.95, so the ratio part holds and the values part does not (means 22.5 and 22.9%), which would make the claim partially reproduced.
deviations: Assumed the offline_move_onset_time column as the movement onset (see fig3-independent-of-curvature).

outcomes.statement: In J-array the first three jPCA planes found within the top 10 PCs capture 22%, 19% and 12% of the variance (54% together), against 64% for the top six PCs, and each plane holds rotations coherent across conditions.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Figure 4
outcomes.quote: All three planes contained rotational structure that was coherent (in the same direction and at a similar angular velocity) across conditions ... The top three jPCA planes (spanning six dimensions) captured 60% (monkey B) and 54% ... the top six PCs ... captured 72% and 64% of the variance
outcomes.notes: With jPCA on the top 10 PCs of J-array, the first three planes capture 13.3%, 13.3% and 12.2% (38.8% together), and the top six PCs 51.9%; only the third plane is within tolerance. The rotations are coherent in each plane, with 98%, 97% and 92% of conditions counter-clockwise, at 1.63, 1.24 and 0.79 Hz. The four readings agree (three planes 37.7 to 38.8%, top six PCs 51.9 to 54.0%).
deviations: Planes are ordered by the magnitude of their M_skew eigenvalues (Methods, "the plane defined by the eigenvectors associated with the largest two (complex-conjugate) imaginary eigenvalues"), and each is oriented as the first.

outcomes.statement: Every dataset contains two, and usually three, planes with rotations, together capturing 50 to 70% of the variance.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Figure 4 legend; Results, Controls regarding rotational structure, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Together these captured 50–70% of the total data variance ... all datasets contained two, and usually three, planes that captured rotations
outcomes.notes: In N-array the three planes capture 47.7% (19.6, 16.2 and 11.9%), inside 45 to 77%, with 97% and 100% of conditions rotating in the first two planes (94% in the third). In J-array they capture 38.8%, below 45%, although 98% and 97% rotate. The four readings agree (J-array 37.7 to 38.8%, N-array 45.8 to 48.8%).

outcomes.statement: The distribution of the angle between the neural state and its derivative in the first jPCA plane, over all conditions and times, peaks near pi/2 (rotation), not near 0.
outcomes.source: Figure 6a
outcomes.quote: The neural data and the generator model have distributions with peaks near π/2
outcomes.notes: The 36-bin histogram of the angle between the state and its derivative in the first plane (2160 angles per dataset) peaks at 0.528 pi in J-array and 0.639 pi in N-array under the main reading; under the four readings at 0.528 to 0.583 pi and 0.639 pi. 69% (J-array) and 82% (N-array) of the angles lie within 0.25 pi of pi/2.

outcomes.statement: For the neural data the rotational (skew-symmetric) dynamics matrix fits the data nearly as well as the best unconstrained linear dynamics matrix, both in the 6-D space and in the first jPCA plane.
outcomes.source: Results, Population-level quantification, paragraph 2; Figure 6b
outcomes.quote: For the neural data and generator model, the fit provided by Mskew was nearly as good as the fit provided by the best unconstrained M (fig. 6b) ... Results were similar whether we considered all six dimensions or just the plane with the strongest rotations
outcomes.notes: In 6-D, R2 is 0.415 for M and 0.381 for M_skew in J-array (ratio 0.918), and 0.580 and 0.527 in N-array (ratio 0.909). In the first plane the ratios are 0.946 and 0.953. Under the four readings and with 24 ms smoothing, the 6-D ratios are 0.870 to 0.931 and the plane ratios 0.908 to 0.975. The paper's figure shows 6-D ratios of about 0.75 to 0.9; the R2 values themselves are not stated in the paper.
deviations: In the plane, M and M_skew are 2 x 2 matrices fitted to the projection onto the first plane (Figure 6b legend, "the rank 2 matrices that capture dynamics in the first jPCA plane").

outcomes.statement: The rotations are brief and fast, up to about 2.5 Hz; the largest eigenvalues of M_skew in the monkey A and B datasets are 8.8 to 13.5 radians/s.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching, paragraph 5, and Population-level quantification, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Their brevity and high frequency (up to ~2.5 Hz) makes them easy to miss ... the largest eigenvalues of Mskew were actually slightly smaller for fast reaches (8.8 versus 9.8 radians/s for monkey A, 12.2 versus 13.5 radians/s for monkey B)
outcomes.notes: The largest eigenvalue of M_skew is 8.44 rad/s (1.344 Hz) in J-array and 8.81 rad/s (1.402 Hz) in N-array, inside 1.26 to 2.75 Hz; the measured value given is the larger. With the range over -1000 to +700 ms, 1.333 and 1.416 Hz. Under the move_begins readings J-array gives 1.063 to 1.098 Hz, below the range, which would make the claim partially reproduced. With 24 ms smoothing, 1.290 and 1.372 Hz. The paper's own values for the array datasets are not stated.
deviations: Assumed the offline_move_onset_time column as the movement onset (see fig3-independent-of-curvature); under move_begins_time the outcome would be partially reproduced.
The derivative is the difference of samples 10 ms apart (Methods), so eigenvalues per sample are multiplied by 100 to give rad/s.

outcomes.statement: Three shuffle controls that keep preparatory activity and invert or reassign the peri-movement activity largely remove the rotational structure found by jPCA, so jPCA does not find rotations that are not there.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Figures 2 and 3; Results, Controls regarding rotational structure, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Multiple ‘shuffle’ controls demonstrate that jPCA does not find rotational structure when such structure is not present ... largely lost following shuffling
outcomes.notes: Dividing points -277 ms (J-array) and -268 ms (N-array) from movement onset. In J-array the original R2(M_skew) is 0.381; no shuffled run reaches it, and the medians are 0.01 (shuffle 1), 0.63 (shuffle 2) and 0.75 (shuffle 3, 0.745) of it, so all three shuffles meet the criterion. In N-array the original is 0.527, and the medians are 0.01, 0.76 and 0.87 of it, so only shuffle 1 meets it. The partial outcome (all three shuffles in one dataset) holds under each of the five seeds (J-array shuffle-3 medians 0.725 to 0.745 of the original, N-array 0.850 to 0.866). With the range over -1000 to +700 ms the outcome is also partial (J-array shuffle 3 at 0.77, N-array shuffle 2 at 0.74); under the two move_begins readings it is not reproduced, as J-array shuffle 3 is at 0.77 to 0.79 and N-array meets only shuffle 1. After shuffles 2 and 3 the median share of conditions rotating counter-clockwise stays at 93 to 98% and the R2 ratio at 0.86 to 0.94; after shuffle 1 it is 58 to 61% and 0.09 to 0.16. The claim's statement that the shuffles largely remove the rotational structure holds for shuffle 1 only in N-array. The Supplementary Figure 2 legend says shuffles 2 and 3 are not expected to remove all rotational structure; whether R2(M_skew) is the right measure for them is asked of a reader (questions/churchland-2012.yaml).
deviations: Shuffle 1 inverts exactly half of the conditions (54 of 108) per unit, drawn at random (Supplementary Figure 2 legend). Inversion reflects each rate after the dividing point about its value there, and reassignment adds the other condition's change from its dividing-point rate to this condition's rate at that point (legend, "simply appended to the final firing rate during the preparatory state, such that there was no discontinuity").
Assumed the offline_move_onset_time column as the movement onset (see fig3-independent-of-curvature); under move_begins_time the outcome would be not reproduced.

outcomes.statement: Analysed separately, the PMd and M1 arrays each show clear rotations; the jPCA plane captures 29% (PMd) and 29% (M1) in J-array and 32% and 28% in N-array.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Figure 5
outcomes.quote: Both PMd and M1 exhibited clear rotations of the neural state
outcomes.notes: With units split by electrode group (group 1 described as the PMd array, group 2 as M1, 96 units each), the first plane captures 21.6% (PMd) and 20.2% (M1) in J-array and 17.7% and 27.1% in N-array; only N-array M1 is within tolerance, and N-array PMd is below 18%, so the partial reading fails as well. Each array rotates (96%, 99%, 91% and 97% of conditions counter-clockwise). The four readings agree (N-array PMd 17.6 to 17.9%). The N-9-10-2010 variant (sub-Nitschke ses-20100910) gives 14.7% (PMd) and 20.8% (M1) against 26% and 24%, with 94% rotating in each.

outcomes.statement: The angular velocity of the rotations is slightly higher for M1 than for PMd in each dataset.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Figure 5 legend
outcomes.quote: Second, the angular velocity of the rotations was in each case slightly higher for M1
outcomes.notes: The first-plane frequency is 2.020 Hz for M1 against 0.844 Hz for PMd in J-array, and 1.488 against 0.973 Hz in N-array. Under the four readings M1 is higher by 1.059 to 1.176 Hz (J-array) and 0.433 to 0.523 Hz (N-array). The N-9-10-2010 variant agrees (1.659 against 1.063 Hz). The paper calls the difference slight; here M1 is 2.39 (J-array) and 1.53 (N-array) times faster under the main reading, and 1.41 to 2.39 times under the four readings.

outcomes.statement: A simulated population of units tuned to hand velocity and speed, with preparatory activity tuned to reach endpoint, matched to the recorded data, shows no robust or consistent rotations; M_skew fits it poorly and its angle distribution peaks slightly above zero.
outcomes.source: Results, Rotations, kinematics and EMG, paragraph 1; Results, Population-level quantification, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 4d and 4h; Figure 6a and 6b
outcomes.quote: For velocity-model populations, jPCA found no robust or consistent rotations (fig. 4a,d,h) ... the velocity-tuned model, the complex-kinematic model, and EMG all had distributions that peaked slightly above zero ... For the velocity-tuned and complex kinematic models, Mskew performed poorly
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading (rates lead the hand by 100 ms, preparatory term falling as the movement term starts) M_skew fits the simulated population poorly in both datasets, with 6-D ratios of 0.590 (J-array) and 0.153 (N-array), below 0.6 and below the neural 0.918 and 0.909. The N-array angle distribution peaks at 0.083 pi, below pi/4, and the J-array one at 0.472 pi, above it, so the criterion holds in N-array only. All five seeds give partially reproduced (J-array 6-D ratios 0.517 to 0.590 and peaks 0.472 to 0.528 pi; N-array ratios 0.134 to 0.174 and peaks 0.083 to 0.139 pi). Under the main reading 28% (J-array) and 39% (N-array) of the simulated angles lie within pi/4 of zero, against 36% and 36% within pi/4 of pi/2. The other readings differ. With the preparatory term falling around hand onset (100 ms lead) the outcome is not reproduced (peaks 0.417 and 0.639 pi), as with a persisting term and a 100 ms lead (0.639 and 0.417 pi; one seed of five gives partially reproduced) and with a persisting term and no lead (0.250 and 0.361 pi); with no lead and the falling term it is reproduced under every seed (peaks -0.083 to 0.028 pi and 0.028 to 0.083 pi). The stricter reading of the peak, 0 <= peak < pi/4, changes only the reading with no lead and the falling term, to partially reproduced. The part of the statement that M_skew fits poorly holds under every reading and seed (6-D ratios 0.056 to 0.590). The simulated population is this attempt's construction from the Methods' description.
deviations: The Methods give the factors (velocity, speed; endpoint and peak speed for the preparatory activity), uniform preferred directions, rates and trial counts matched to the recorded units, and gamma-interval spiking of order 2. They do not give how far the rates lead the hand, the time course of the preparatory term, or the factors' relative weights. Assumed a lead of 100 ms, the usual lead of motor cortical activity over the hand in velocity-tuning models such as the one the paper cites (ref. 27), and a preparatory term that falls to zero over 100 ms centred on the time the movement term starts (100 ms before hand onset), since in the model both terms are neural activity and preparatory activity gives way when movement activity begins. The first version of this attempt centred the fall on hand onset, which with the 100 ms lead overlaps the two terms inside the analysed window; it was changed after round 1 of verification, before the new reading was run, and is kept as a reading. A lead of 0 ms and a persisting preparatory term are the other readings. Factors are scaled to unit SD and weighted by uniform draws on 0 to 1 (Methods, "a random combination of the underlying factors").
Each simulated unit's noiseless rate is scaled to the recorded unit's mean and range over -1000 to +700 ms and rectified; the paper says only that firing rates were matched.
Simulated with the condition-mean hand paths of the session (smoothed with a 20 ms Gaussian before differentiating), under the main pipeline reading only.

The criterion's "angle peak is below pi/4" is read as |peak| < pi/4, a peak near zero; a peak near -pi, where the state and its derivative point in opposite directions, does not count. The stricter 0 <= peak < pi/4 is shown as well.

outcomes.statement: A simulated population tuned to hand position, velocity, acceleration and jerk (with the Methods' sensitivities) produces multiphasic responses but no consistent rotations; M_skew fits it poorly.
outcomes.source: Results, Rotations, kinematics and EMG, paragraph 1; Results, Population-level quantification, paragraph 2; Figure 4e and 4i; Figure 6a and 6b
outcomes.quote: This model produced multiphasic responses but not consistent rotations (fig. 4b,e,i) ... For the velocity-tuned and complex kinematic models, Mskew performed poorly
outcomes.notes: Under the main reading M_skew fits poorly in both datasets (6-D ratios 0.074 in J-array and 0.060 in N-array, against the neural 0.918 and 0.909), but neither angle distribution peaks near zero: the peaks are at -0.972 pi (J-array) and 0.806 pi (N-array), with 11% and 10% of the angles within pi/4 of zero. All five seeds give not reproduced (J-array peaks of magnitude 0.528 to 0.972 pi, N-array 0.750 to 0.972 pi; 6-D ratios 0.071 to 0.078 and 0.060 to 0.069). Under the claim's seed the other readings give not reproduced, except no lead with the falling preparatory term, which gives partially reproduced under every seed (J-array peaks 0.028 to 0.139 pi, N-array 0.250 to 0.306 pi). No lead with a persisting term gives not reproduced under the claim's seed and partially reproduced under three of the five seeds (J-array peaks -0.917, -0.917, 0.083, 0.139 and 0.139 pi). The stricter reading of the peak, 0 <= peak < pi/4, gives the same outcomes. The part of the statement that M_skew fits poorly holds under every reading and seed (6-D ratios 0.060 to 0.398). The first version of this attempt gave partially reproduced, counting the J-array peak at -0.972 pi as below pi/4.
deviations: Uses the Methods' sensitivities (25, 10, 1 and 0.05 spikes/s per m, m/s, m/s2 and m/s3 along the preferred direction). The preparatory term, "sensitive to target endpoint", is given 25 spikes/s per m of endpoint along a preparatory preferred direction, an assumption. The lead, the preparatory time course and the reading of the angle peak are as for fig6-velocity-model.

outcomes.statement: The population responses of the swimming leech and of premotor cortex in a walking monkey rotate in the jPCA plane, as expected for rhythmic movement.
outcomes.source: Results, Rhythmic responses in different systems, paragraph 1; Figure 1a, 1b, 1d and 1e
outcomes.quote: We projected the population response onto a two-dimensional state space and found rotations of the neural state for both the swimming leech (fig. 1d; projection of 164 simultaneously recorded neurons) and the walking monkey
outcomes.notes: The leech optical recordings and the walking-monkey recordings are not in the dandiset, which holds only delayed-reach Utah-array sessions (all ten files were read). The paper says the leech data were recorded by K. Briggman and W. Kristan and gives no public location for either.

outcomes.statement: Single neurons recorded with single electrodes show multiphasic, quasi-oscillatory responses lasting about 1 to 1.5 cycles, from 469 isolations in four monkeys averaging 810 trials per neuron.
outcomes.source: Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 1c and Figure 2
outcomes.quote: We analyzed 469 single-neuron recordings from motor and premotor cortex of four monkeys (A,B,J,N) ... Yet there appear to be oscillations in many single-neuron responses, beginning just before movement onset and lasting for ~1–1.5 cycles
outcomes.notes: The 469 single-electrode isolations of monkeys A, B, J and N are not in the dandiset, whose ten files are array sessions with unsorted threshold crossings.

outcomes.statement: The rotations are seen in the seven single-electrode datasets (monkeys A, B, J1 to J4 and N), for example monkey B, A, J3 and N in Figure 3a to 3d.
outcomes.source: Figure 3a to 3d; Results, Quasi-rhythmic responses during reaching, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: The resulting projections (fig. 3a-f) show four striking features. First, rotations of the neural state are prevalent during reaching
outcomes.notes: The seven single-electrode datasets (A, B, J1 to J4 and N) are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: The recorded muscle populations (6 to 12 EMG recordings per dataset) show weak, inconsistent rotations, also when the neural population is down-sampled to their size.
outcomes.source: Results, Rotations, kinematics and EMG, paragraph 1; Figure 4c, 4f and 4j; Figure 6a and 6b; Supplementary Figure 6
outcomes.quote: Although EMG is strongly multiphasic, the population of muscles did not show consistent rotations (fig. 4c,f,j, summary data below). This was not due to the smaller size of the muscle population (supplementary fig. 6)
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds no EMG; the paper recorded EMG only for the single-electrode datasets.

outcomes.statement: A generator model of two rotations of fixed frequency fits deltoid EMG with correlations of 0.97 to 0.99, and its simulated units resemble real neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Rotations, kinematics and EMG, paragraphs 3 and 5; Figure 5; Supplementary Figures 7 to 9
outcomes.quote: This ‘generator model’ provided excellent EMG fits (fig. 5b,c; supplementary fig. 7,8). The fit/EMG correlation ranged from 0.97–0.99 across datasets ... Simulated units displayed multiphasic response patterns resembling those of real neurons
outcomes.notes: The generator model is fitted to deltoid EMG, which is not in the dandiset; the paper says it could not be simulated for the array datasets.

outcomes.statement: Rotations have similar angular velocity for instructed fast and slow reaches; the largest M_skew eigenvalues are 8.8 against 9.8 radians/s (monkey A) and 12.2 against 13.5 (monkey B), with larger amplitude for fast reaches.
outcomes.source: Results, Population-level quantification, paragraph 3; Figure 6c and 6d

findings.statement: The Units tables of all ten files hold unsorted threshold crossings, one unit per electrode (192 per session), as their description says, where the paper analysed 146 (J-array) and 218 (N-array) sorted single and multi-unit isolations. The sorted isolations are not in the dandiset. On these units the first jPCA plane captures 14.9% and 22.9% of the variance, against the paper's average of 28%.

The dandiset holds the paper's two array datasets (sub-Jenkins ses-20090918 and sub-Nitschke ses-20100923) and eight further array sessions, one of which (sub-Nitschke ses-20100910) matches the N-9-10-2010 session of Supplementary Figure 5. The seven single-electrode datasets, the EMG, the leech and walking-monkey recordings and the J-11-06-2009 session of Supplementary Figure 5 are not in it. Six of the paper's 22 claims cannot be tested.

Two sessions, sub-Nitschke ses-20100920 and ses-20100922, have no maze_condition, correct_reach, trial_version, active_target, proto_trial, novel_maze or unhittable columns, which the other eight files have, so their trials cannot be grouped by condition or selected for consistent reaches as in the paper. The paper does not use these sessions.

The trial table has two movement-onset columns, move_begins_time (described only as "movement onset time") and offline_move_onset_time ("movement onset time, calculated offline using a robust algorithm"), which differ by a median of 25 ms in J-array and 52 ms in N-array. Nothing says which one is the onset the paper aligned on, and several results change with it (the variance captured by the jPCA plane, 14.9 against 18.7% in J-array, and its frequency, 1.344 against 1.098 Hz). The hand speed starts to rise at offline_move_onset_time (median 43 and 15 mm/s); at move_begins_time it is already 137 and 160 mm/s. The choice changes the outcomes of five claims.

The spikes of both arrays are consistent with the clock of the trial table. Reach direction decodes at chance from each array before target onset (0.12 to 0.17 against 0.14 to 0.17 with shuffled labels) and above it after target onset (0.37 to 0.70). The lag between the arrays' movement-related changes is constant across six blocks of each session (-4 to 11 ms in J-array, 25 to 32 ms in N-array, M1 later), so there is no drift like that of the LFP's second, slower clock. After target onset, an event that does not depend on the movement onset, the arrays respond nearly together (M1 lag -4 ms in J-array and 9 ms in N-array, half-rise of the across-condition spread at 99 and 101 ms in N-array), so a fixed offset of 25 ms or more between the N-array arrays' clocks is not supported; the later M1 change around movement is consistent with a later M1 response.

Checks that passed. No recording is deposited twice (the trial-interval and spike-count hashes of the ten files all differ). Spike times are sorted within every unit and every analysis window lies inside its trial. Hand position is in mm with a conversion to metres, its speed rises at offline_move_onset_time, and the hand ends a median 9.1 mm (J-array) and 11.4 mm (N-array) from the hit target minus the cursor offset. Electrode groups 1 and 2 are described as the PMd and M1 arrays, 96 units each.

Nothing in the dandiset's metadata or its files says which of the ten sessions are the paper's datasets. The dandiset description names only the areas, the arrays and the task, every session_description is empty, and no file names J-array, N-array or any other dataset of the paper. The two array datasets can be found only by their dates (sub-Jenkins ses-20090918 and sub-Nitschke ses-20100923), and the eight other sessions (five 27-condition maze sessions, two without condition columns, and sub-Nitschke ses-20100910 with 108 conditions) are not described.

outcomes.note: Version 0.261122.2046 adds the trial column offline_move_onset_time, which the blind attempt took as movement onset; version 0.260528.0919 has only move_begins_time, which the earlier attempt used. On move_begins_time the blind attempt's J-array plane captures 18.7 to 19.0%, inside 18 to 38.5% like the earlier 20.0%, and the earlier attempt's code run here on the new version gives 19.98% in J-array on move_begins_time and 16.67% on offline_move_onset_time.

The value part fails in both. The ratio part turns on the onset column the new version adds; in J-array the jPCA plane captures 0.78 of the PC2 and PC3 variance on offline_move_onset_time and 0.84 to 0.95 on move_begins_time (earlier 0.93), and the earlier attempt's code on the new version gives 0.925 and 0.778.

J-array decides it. On the new offline_move_onset_time column the blind attempt gets 1.344 Hz, inside 1.26 to 2.75 Hz, and on move_begins_time 1.063 to 1.098 Hz, below it like the earlier 1.03 Hz; the earlier attempt's code on the new version gives 1.033 Hz on move_begins_time and 1.447 Hz on offline_move_onset_time.

J-array shuffle 3 decides it. Aligned on the new offline_move_onset_time column its median is 0.745 of the original R2(M_skew), just inside the 0.75 limit (0.725 to 0.745 over five seeds), and on move_begins_time 0.77 to 0.79, outside it like the earlier 0.81, which makes the blind attempt's move_begins readings not reproduced as well. The two attempts' shuffles follow the same legend, and the dividing points differ only by the onset (-277 and -268 ms against -301 and -320 ms).

N-array PMd decides it against the 18% floor, at 18.1% in the earlier attempt and 17.6 to 17.9% under the blind attempt's four readings. Run on the new version, the earlier code gives 18.16% on move_begins_time, and 17.70% when the rates are computed over a longer span and the range is still taken over -800 to +500 ms, because earlier-entry/reach.py (condition_rates, then jpca) takes each unit's normalisation range over the whole rate window, whose first and last bins are Gaussian-smoothed with mode nearest from single 1 ms bins.

Both simulate rates leading the hand by 100 ms. Under the blind attempt's main reading the angle peaks are 0.472 pi (J-array) and 0.083 pi (N-array), so the criterion holds in N-array; with the fall centred on hand onset, its first reading, close to the earlier decay, they are 0.417 and 0.639 pi and the claim is not reproduced, as in the earlier attempt (0.806 and 0.361 pi). The blind attempt changed its main reading after round 1 of verification, as its record says.

disagreements.reason: The notebook gets partial only because J's angle peak of -0.972 pi counts as "below pi/4". A peak near +-pi is not "slightly above zero"; sim_ok tests peak_over_pi < 0.25 without wrapping, so any negative peak passes (problem 1). Corrected, both datasets fail on the angle peak under the main reading, though the 6-D ratios are low (0.095 and 0.144) as the paper predicts.

paper_notes.statement: Question for the paper's authors. Which movement onset were the array datasets aligned on, the rig's online detection (move_begins_time in the files) or the offline estimate (offline_move_onset_time), and over which times was each neuron's firing-rate range taken for the soft normalisation? The paper says the data were precisely aligned on movement onset. This attempt assumed the offline estimate and the analysed window; with the online onset the outcomes of five claims would change (fig3-independent-of-curvature, var-captured-jpc-plane, pc23-variance, rotation-frequency and suppfig3-shuffle-controls), while the range window changes none.

Question for the paper's authors. For the velocity and complex kinematic models, how far did the simulated rates lead the hand, what was the time course of the preparatory term (did it end when the movement term began, at hand onset, or persist), and how were the factors weighted? With a 100 ms lead and a preparatory term ending as the movement term begins, the simulated velocity population's angle distribution peaks at 0.47 pi (J-array) and 0.08 pi (N-array); with the term ending at hand onset at 0.42 and 0.64 pi; with no lead and the falling term near 0 in both (-0.08 and 0.08 pi); with no lead and a persisting term at 0.25 and 0.36 pi. M_skew fits poorly under every choice.

entries.name: churchland-2012
entries.title: Rotational population dynamics during reaching (Churchland et al. 2012)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Churchland, Cunningham, Kaufman, Foster, Nuyujukian, Ryu and Shenoy (2012) on dandiset 000070, which holds the paper's two Utah-array datasets (J-array and N-array, 108 maze conditions each) as unsorted threshold crossings. It runs jPCA on the condition-averaged rates and tests the direction, phase, variance and frequency of the rotations, the fits of the skew-symmetric dynamics, the shuffle controls, the split by array and two simulated kinematic populations. The single-electrode, EMG, leech and walking-monkey data are not in the dandiset.
